    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 30 min read (6097 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~30 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that AI evaluations help shape which systems people build, adopt, and trust.
    • In a recent development, open source offers a means to build stronger, more frequently updated, and more comparable evaluations and the infrastructure around them.
    • The Hugging Face hub is the home for AI evaluation: we host around 3500 eval leaderboards and have seen about a 16X growth in eval datasets on the hub in the past year, to about 17000 datasets.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that AI evaluations help shape which systems people build, adopt, and trust. An evaluation gives a system tasks, checks its answers or actions, and produces a score. Building and maintaining a useful evaluation therefore takes real work: defining tasks that reflect domain expertise, scoring them reliably, and checking that the results support the claims made. When methods, code, and data stay private, that work is harder for others to scrutinize or build on.

    In a recent development, open source offers a means to build stronger, more frequently updated, and more comparable evaluations and the infrastructure around them. Existing tasks, environments, and tools give builders a starting point, so their effort can go to domain expertise and validation. Sharing how an evaluation was built, including what went wrong, lets others find errors, improve it, and reuse it.

    The Hugging Face hub is the home for AI evaluation: we host around 3500 eval leaderboards and have seen about a 16X growth in eval datasets on the hub in the past year, to about 17000 datasets. In recent months, we have also incorporated support for agentic abstractions that are relevant to evaluation. For example, Traces that store an agent’s work in an easily reviewable and sharable way; Benchmarks that highlight datasets used to evaluate models with leaderboards; and Environments that show datasets used as agentic RL or evaluation environments.

    It has been revealed that in the research community, AI evaluation terminology is notoriously inconsistent. The glossary at the end defines each term we use and notes the other names you may come across.

    AI evaluation design has evolved in three forms as language models have become more capable and able to perform more complex work: question answer, agentic, and teams or swarms. Question-answer benchmarks such as MMLU (2020) and GPQA (2023) measure knowledge and reasoning through the answers models produce. As models became capable of planning and using tools, agentic benchmarks such as SWE-bench and WebArena expanded the scope to resolving software complications and completing tasks on websites. These tasks require evaluation setups that account for the environment in which the system operates and the changes it makes.

    Lately, research on multi-agent systems has started to add another dimension: how agents coordinate and what they accomplish together. This includes decentralized swarms, teams managed by an orchestrator, and specialized agents collaborating on scientific work. Figure 1 shows a rough timeline of these three eras of evaluations.

    Figure 1. Three types of language model evals. Question-and-answer benchmarks check a response against a key. Agentic benchmarks check what an agent changed in an environment. Team and swarm benchmarks score what a group of agents produced.

    According to recent reports, we’ll focus on agentic evaluations in this article for two reasons. First, they are becoming increasingly the most prominent type in model release announcements due to high user and enterprise interest in agentic deployment. Second, they offer a useful starting point for understanding how evaluation design affects model performance. Team and swarm evaluations introduce further complexity through interactions between agents, which we leave outside the scope of this guide. Once an agent uses tools to complete a task, each part of the surrounding software can affect its score. For instance, in an audit of Terminal-Bench, researchers kept the model fixed and changed the agent harness. Accuracy varied by up to 29.9 percentage points. To understand differences like that, we examine the anatomy of an agentic evaluation and follow one task from the instructions the agent receives to the checks that determine whether it passed.

    Figure 2. The different components of an agentic evaluation.

    There are various parts to an agentic evaluation. A task gives the agent its instruction. The agent harness wraps the model and its tools, letting it work inside a pinned environment. During one rollout, the agent attempts the task from start to finish: it may run several commands, inspect their output, and try again before it stops. The evaluation harness runs several rollouts for each task. When a rollout ends, the verifier grades the environment's final state. Each rollout also leaves a trace, and traces and scores together become part of the final published evidence. Each part can be published, inspected, and reused separately.

    Demand for independent evaluation is growing. Policymakers, enterprises, and researchers want evaluations they can verify, and today they mostly cannot: 98.2% of model-benchmark scores are reported by only one party, and researchers have argued that in-house evaluation is not enough.

    According to recent reports, at the same time, more benchmarks are holding back test items to reduce contamination: questions or solutions entering training data, so scores may reflect prior exposure. Artificial Analysis says 60% of its Intelligence Index v5, revealed in October 2026, rests on evaluations with private test sets or held-out answers. Google DeepMind recently piloted double-blind evaluations, where a secure enclave hides an outside evaluator's test prompts from the model provider and the model's weights from the evaluator. While that can reduce contamination, privacy by itself does not guarantee quality, and withholding supporting materials can make expert review harder. We argue that builders can and should still share infrastructure, grading methods, and evidence about task design. Scrutiny depends on giving others a way to question the measurement and correct mistakes, including controlled review where public release is unsuitable.

    Industry observers note that with the anatomy in place, we now build one agentic evaluation for a real use case: an agent that analyzes measurements for a physics lab. Rather than starting from scratch, we adapt an open task, so most of our effort goes into domain expertise and validation.

    We work through eight steps: define the claim, find a task, run it unchanged, adapt it, check the evaluation, read the traces, report the score, and compare models. We then take stock of what we reused. The full walkthrough is in Appendix A. Figure 3 maps the steps and what each produced in our example.

    Figure 3. The eight steps of building an agentic evaluation. The left panel highlights each step in turn, and the right panel shows what it involved in our example. Yellow steps work on the evaluation itself, and orange steps run models and read the results.

    Recent findings suggest that claim. Consider a physics lab that wants an agent to fit peaks in a Raman spectrum. A Raman spectrum is a measurement whose peaks reveal properties of a material, here graphene. The agent's job is ordinary coding: read the data file, fit a curve to each peak, and save the results (Figure 5 in Appendix A). For the purposes of this article, our claim is deliberately narrow: fit the specified peaks, calculate the requested D-to-G ratio (the intensity of one peak relative to another, which can indicate defects in the material; we also call it the defect ratio), and save accurate results consistently. Reviewing a whole lab report would need additional skills and evidence.

    Starting task and baseline. We reused the Harbor task format and Terminal-Bench's raman-fitting task. Harbor is an open source evaluation harness, and Terminal-Bench is an open benchmark of tasks that an agent completes in a terminal. We first ran the task's reference solution, which passed, and then ran the original task three times with Terminus-2, a terminal agent harness, and gpt-oss-120b, an open-weight model from OpenAI. Harbor ran inside an HF Job, each rollout used its own HF Sandbox, and Inference Providers supplied the model responses. Reusing the runner and task format let us concentrate on the physics, grading, and review. Only the agent harness needed no fresh work. Every other component needed checking or new work, which we list part by part at the end of Appendix A.

    Sources indicate that adaptation. We built raman-lab: eight synthetic spectra with known parameters and varied noise and defect levels. The adaptation fits three peaks instead of two and reports a defect ratio. We used an agent to help generate the spectra, reviewed them by hand, and wrote new instructions, reference fits, and output checks. The new instructions state the units and parameter definitions that the original left implicit. These eight tasks are a development set, meaning tasks we use while building the evaluation; broader coverage should follow the variation in real measurements.

    Checks. Before executing more model runs, we tested the evaluation itself. We ran the reference solution, an agent that does nothing, and a shortcut that skips the required work. The reference solution should pass every task, and the other two should fail. Our shortcut read the height of each peak straight from the data and guessed the widths. It returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks without fitting the spectra, so we added checks on the fit itself.

    It has been revealed that shortcut. We also tested a shortcut to check how robust the evaluation is against cheating. Our shortcut is a short script that skips the actual fitting. It reads the tallest point of each peak straight from the data, guesses the peak widths, and divides the D height by the G height. Even so, it returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks, so a grader that checked only the ratio would have given it full marks. We added checks on each fitted peak, and the final verifier rejects it.

    Recent findings suggest that figure 4. What we learned by measuring different aspects while building the evaluation. (A) Testing the grader with a shortcut showed that a ratio-only check could be fooled. (B) Reading gpt-oss-120b’s traces showed that most of its failures came from stopping early. (C) Running other models showed that the tasks can be solved. Appendix A has the detailed results in Figure 7 (how gpt-oss-120b’s attempts ended), Figure 8 (all six models) and Figure 9 (when each model said it was done).

    Industry observers note that baseline. On the original task, gpt-oss-120b passed 0 of 3 rollouts. In two it declared completion before observing relevant output; in the third it could not read the data file, which uses decimal commas that the reference solution converts before loading. The score alone could not tell these failures from an incorrect fit. The traces could.

    Sources indicate that traces and score. On the eight adapted tasks, we ran three rollouts per task. The adapted setup passed 11 of 24 rollouts. In 19, the model called mark_task_complete in its first response; 11 of those attempts produced no results file. Several of these began with a script failing because NumPy or SciPy was missing, which the task expects the agent to install. Most failures therefore came from stopping early or from a missing package, and only two of the 13 failed the fit check (Figure 7 in Appendix A). Our pass@3 was 7/8: seven tasks succeeded at least once. Our pass^3 was 1/8: one task succeeded every time. Retries may be acceptable when a person reviews the output. Unattended processing needs consistency, so the second measure matters more. The mean pass rate was 0.46, with a standard error of about 0.11 when rollouts are clustered by task. A repeat run passed 10 of 24. With eight development tasks, we would be cautious about generalizing either result to new spectra.

    Model comparison. We then compared six models on the same eight tasks (Figure 4). Several providers can serve the same open-weight model with different quantization and context limits, so we pinned one provider per model. With DeepInfra pinned as the provider, gpt-oss-120b passed 13 of 24 rollouts, compared with 11 of 24 in the earlier run, which used the default provider. Only gpt-oss-120b declared completion in its first response, in 22 of 24 rollouts. None of the other five models did so in any rollout (Figure 9 in Appendix A). The comparison also shows the limits of the development set. Qwen3.8-27B, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and MiniMax-M3.1-Flash passed all 24 raman-lab rollouts, so these tasks cannot rank them. That will take harder tasks.

    According to recent reports, our shortcut returned the expected defect ratio without fitting a spectrum. A verifier that checked only the ratio would have given it full marks on all eight tasks. We found it by trying to break the grader with a solution we knew was incomplete, then added checks on the fitted spectrum (Appendix A, Step 5).

    The shortcut got the right answer for the wrong reason, like a student who copies the final number without the working. The lesson for us was to test what the output demonstrates. A faster valid method should pass; a method that skips a required skill should not. Domain experts can help set tolerances so the verifier accepts alternative correct fits without accepting work that misses the point of the task.

    Such errors are common, and they move scores considerably. A review of agentic benchmarks found that flaws in task setup or reward design can shift measured performance by up to 100% in relative terms.

    In a recent development, public review can expose errors in instructions and tests that benchmark builders missed. Terminal-Bench 2.1 fixed 28 of its 89 tasks after user reports, including one whose tests expected Spark SQL while its instructions asked for PostgreSQL, and agent rankings stayed stable through the correction.

    Recent findings suggest that access to the evidence also determines how much work an outside audit takes. CritPt keeps its reference solutions private, so the physicists who audited it had to solve the problems themselves before finding errors in 21 of the 56 challenges they reviewed. The authors then released a corrected version. OpenAI's audit of SWE-bench Verified found material issues in 59.4% of the 138 problems it examined, working from tasks and tests that anyone can read. For a builder, outside scrutiny is part of validation: publish what reviewers need to challenge a task, give them a way to report problems, and record what changed.

    Similar flaws emerged in SWE-bench Pro. In July 2026 OpenAI estimated that about 30% of SWE-Bench Pro tasks were broken and withdrew its recommendation to adopt it. Benchmark validation needs to continue after release.

    Recent findings suggest that A consistent score can still measure the wrong thing. Measuring what Matters, a review of 445 LLM benchmarks by 29 expert reviewers, found recurring patterns in tasks and metrics that undermine construct validity: whether the tasks and metrics support claims about the intended capability.

    For example, fitting synthetic spectra does not establish that an agent can review lab reports. That may also require recognizing a poor measurement or asking for help. If every task supplies a usable spectrum, the test cannot show whether the agent knows when a fit would be inappropriate.

    Recent findings suggest that harder Than the Task extends this concern to organizational work, where authority, distributed knowledge, and dependencies can decide success. Its authors find that fewer than one quarter of prominent benchmarks claim to cover any such dimension. An agent may need calibration data from another team or permission to replace a measurement, and supplying everything at the outset removes those difficulties. If they matter to the claim, they belong in the evaluation. If they do not, it is enough to say that they remain untested.

    Each error is worth a short record: the failed assumption, how it was found, and what changed. The record should also name the affected versions and say whether earlier scores remain comparable.

    The SWE-bench Verified audit described above also found contamination: every frontier model tested could reproduce the reference patch or verbatim problem details for some tasks. SWE-bench's public repositories and wide use exposed tasks to training. The openness that enabled scrutiny of bad tests also made items easier to encounter before evaluation.

    According to recent reports, however, if contamination is carefully controlled for during training, hiding the test set by itself does not prevent saturation. A study of 60 language model benchmarks found similar saturation in public and private ones, and concluded that hiding test data does not prevent saturation once a benchmark is widely adopted, meaning a good benchmark falls out of use due to saturation without developers being able to learn from and build on it. What did correspond to lower saturation was expert curation and a larger test set.

    This leaves a practical release question: what can we expose for review while protecting active test items?

    Balancing contamination risks against saturation requires a strategic approach to what content is made public. Rather than treating openness as an all-or-nothing decision, benchmark creators can decide what to release part by part, protecting active test tasks from data leakage while still sharing the underlying infrastructure, grading methods, and reference examples that allow external researchers to audit and build upon the evaluation.

    Sources indicate that existing benchmarks show a range of openness. ARC-AGI-2 publishes a training set and a 120-task evaluation set, and holds back semi-private and private sets of 120 tasks each. AILuminate keeps its official prompts confidential, publishes its methods and taxonomy, and keeps the underlying evidence for controlled review by authorized auditors and trusted researchers. Terminal-Bench publishes its tasks and marks their files with a canary string asking that they stay out of training corpora. No public reviewer can check a protected item, so whatever stays closed needs a review route of its own.

    Industry observers note that table 1 outlines the core considerations of open sourcing an evaluation: what can be open, where it lives on the Hugging Face Hub, and what may stay protected. It has one row for each component in Figure 2, so you can go straight to the part you are about to release.

    Industry observers note that table 1. What to open, how to share it on the Hugging Face Hub, and what can stay protected, for each evaluation component.

    Our own example follows this approach. We released raman-lab as a dataset on the Hub. It includes eight synthetic graphene spectra in Harbor task format, each with its environment, reference fit, verifier, and tolerances. The raw rollouts behind our results are shared as a separate dataset including Harbor trial folders with trajectories and verifier output for all six models. The spectrum generator, analysis code, and results are in a companion GitHub repository, so both the agent harness and the evaluation harness can be inspected and rerun.

    Recent findings suggest that in a more sensitive domain, a clinical evaluation could open its environment definition, harness, tool interfaces, and grading framework, with synthetic cases for development use. Patient records and reference answers would stay under controlled access while authorized reviewers inspect disputed judgments. Each restriction should come with a condition for revisiting it.

    Sources indicate that we recommend a short checklist, drawn in part from the more comprehensive Agentic Benchmark Checklist. Before releasing or retiring an evaluation, check that another builder can:.

    These release decisions also determine what remains useful when the benchmark no longer separates the systems it was built to compare.

    Benchmarks have a lifecycle. They are built, adopted, optimized against, and in time stop separating the systems they were made to compare. The saturation study from section 3 rated 29 of its 60 language model benchmarks as highly saturated, with rates rising with age. Saturation is not a failure in itself, since it can mean the capability has arrived.

    According to recent reports, what a benchmark leaves behind depends on how open it was. Publishing only scores leaves future builders little they can run or adapt. When the tasks, environments, verifiers, and traces are open, each keeps working after the leaderboard stops. A solved task becomes a regression check for a latest harness. Its environment and verifier can seed a harder successor. Open benchmarks also get repaired and reissued: MMLU's questions became MMLU-Redux, and Terminal-Bench 2.0 became 2.1 through community contributions. Our own walkthrough is an afterlife of this kind: raman-lab began as one task in a benchmark built for general terminal work.

    Recent findings suggest that that is the promise of building evaluations openly. The work that goes into an evaluation can outlive the benchmark itself, giving others a foundation to ask fresh questions, test new capabilities, and improve on what came before. The more we share what we build and learn, the less each new evaluation has to start from scratch.

    If you’re curious what this looks like in practice, then follow our practical example.

    According to recent reports, consider a physics lab that wants an agent to fit peaks in a Raman spectrum. Raman spectroscopy shines a laser on a sample and measures shifts in the frequency of the scattered light; the resulting peaks reveal properties of the material. For graphene, an atom-thick sheet of carbon, the G and 2D peaks near 1580 and 2700 cm⁻¹ identify the number of layers. A third peak, D, appears when the lattice is disordered, and its intensity relative to G can indicate defects. Figure 5 shows the setup.

    Recent findings suggest that figure 5. Our intended setup. A laser lights a graphene sample, and a spectrometer records how the scattered light has shifted. The agent receives that spectrum as a file, fits a curve to each peak, and saves the fitted values. The verifier checks the saved values against reference fits. The curve shown is a sketch, not measured data.

    Industry observers note that we start by building on a task from an open benchmark. Terminal-Bench 2 already includes raman-fitting: fit a Lorentzian curve, a mathematical peak shape, to each of those two peaks and save eight parameters to /app/results.json. That gives us a runnable starting point for a narrower lab evaluation. We run these on the open source evaluation harness, Harbor. Table 2 lists what the task provides and what to check before reusing each part.

    Sources indicate that table 2. What to check before reusing each component.

    In a recent development, A good place to start is a claim: a plain statement of what the agent can do, which the evaluation is meant to support. "The agent can fit a Raman spectrum" is a claim, and so is "the agent can process a lab report." From there, you can break the claim into smaller skills that can be checked one at a time, such as reading the file, locating the peaks, and writing the output.

    For the purposes of this article, our claim is deliberately narrow: fit the specified peaks, calculate the requested D-to-G ratio, and save accurate results consistently. Reviewing a whole lab report would need additional skills and evidence.

    Domain experts can help here. We suggest asking them to choose realistic noise levels, tolerances, and available software, then score examples independently and investigate disagreements. From there, you can break the claim into parts you can check and map each part to what each task tests.

    According to recent reports, for your own domain, the Hugging Face Hub is a good place to look, under its Benchmark and Environment dataset types. When you find a candidate, it is worth inspecting its instructions, environment, reference solution, and tests. Even a task that models already solve can provide useful infrastructure. From raman-fitting we inherit a working task format. It has only one spectrum, though, and a lab's measurements vary, so we expand on this task further as described in Step 4.

    Before running any model, it helps to run the reference solution (also called oracle). If it fails, the fault lies in the task, environment, or verifier, and needs to be fixed before you read anything into model failures. After that, you can run the model several times without changing the setup.

    We ran Harbor inside an HF Job, which supplied compute for the runner. Each rollout used its own HF Sandbox for commands and files, and Inference Providers supplied the model responses. With Harbor's hf-sandbox extra installed and HF_TOKEN set, these commands test the oracle, then run three rollouts with Terminus-2, a terminal agent harness, and gpt-oss-120b, an open-weight model from OpenAI.

    In these commands, -t names the task, -a the agent, -e the environment, -m the model, and -k the number of rollouts per task.

    The model passed 0 of 3 rollouts. In two it declared completion before observing relevant output; in the third it could not read the data file, which uses decimal commas that the reference solution converts before loading. The score alone could not tell these failures from an incorrect fit. The traces could.

    We built raman-lab: eight synthetic spectra with known parameters and varied noise and defect levels. The adaptation fits three peaks instead of two and reports a defect ratio. We used an agent to help generate the spectra, reviewed them by hand, and wrote upcoming instructions, reference fits, and output checks. These eight tasks are a development set, meaning tasks we use while building the evaluation; broader coverage should follow the variation in real measurements.

    The D-to-G intensity ratio can indicate defects, but its interpretation depends on the laser excitation energy and the disorder regime. An evaluation asking for a "defect ratio" must say which peaks, whether intensity means height or integrated area, and how the result is checked.

    The original instruction.md reveals why such definitions matter: it asks for x0, gamma, amplitude, and offset without defining them or their units. The reference solution treats them as peak center, half-width at half-maximum, height above background, and background level, and converts the x-axis from nanometres to Raman shift. We put choices like these into the adapted instructions, so that the verifier's requirements are visible. Figure 6 shows the two files side by side.

    Recent findings suggest that figure 6. The instruction.md files for raman-fitting and raman-lab, side by side. The highlighted additions cover the new parts of the claim: the D peak, the defect ratio, and both in the saved results. The remaining part, handling varied measurements, lives in the data: all eight raman-lab tasks share this instruction, and only the spectrum, with its noise and defect level, changes.

    The verifier is guided by three rules:.

    The shared format can stay as it is while the data and checks change. This command creates a task scaffold:.

    Before executing more model runs, test the evaluation itself. Here datasets/my-evals contains the adapted tasks.

    Recent findings suggest that our shortcut returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks without fitting the spectra, so we added checks on the fit itself. Section 3 explains what that means for verifier design.

    It is helpful to read both successful and failed rollouts. Harbor records messages, tool calls, and observations in agent/trajectory.json using ATIF, a shared trace format. Grouping failures by cause makes the patterns easier to see: parsing the data, executing a tool, stopping too early, or grading the output.

    Sources indicate that the adapted setup passed 11 of 24 rollouts. In 19, the model called mark_task_complete in its first response; 11 of those attempts produced no results file.

    Figure 7. On 19 of 24 attempts, the agent called mark_task_complete in its first response. Eleven produced no results file, seven passed, and one failed the fit check. Of the five remaining attempts, four passed and one failed the fit check.

    Several missing-file failures began with missing NumPy or SciPy. The published task expects the agent to install them; its reference solution starts with a pip install. A lab evaluation of fitting with supplied tools could install and pin them in advance. Dependencies also drift: Terminal-Bench 2.1 repaired nine tasks whose external dependencies had changed after release.

    Preinstalling changes the evaluation condition, so keep the model, harness, tasks, and rollout count fixed when comparing the two setups.

    Finally, we adapt the setup, repeat the checks in step 5, and rerun. Harbor's trace exporter can prepare records for sharing on the Hub. It is worth reviewing them for protected content first, and keeping both successes and failures so others can investigate the result.

    The right metric depends on the decision you need to make:.

    Retries may be acceptable when a person reviews the output. Unattended processing needs consistency, so the second measure matters more.

    In a recent development, A mean is more useful with its uncertainty beside it. Rollouts of the same spectrum share its difficulty, so they are not independent, and the standard error should be clustered by task. Clustering gave a mean success rate of 0.46 with a standard error of about 0.11. A repeat run passed 10 of 24 rollouts, compared with 11 of 24 in the first run. With only eight development tasks, we would be cautious about generalizing either result to new spectra.

    Harbor writes a result.json per rollout, which it calls a trial. We group these by task, check that each task has three rollouts, and record errors or exclusions. Reporting tokens, elapsed time, and tool calls beside the score lets readers compare setups that reach similar results at different costs.

    Sources indicate that when a single model fails a task, that run alone cannot tell us what went wrong. It could be the model, the agent harness, or the evaluation itself. Running more models on the same tasks helps narrow the possibilities. When several models fail the same task, inspect the instructions, environment, and verifier for a shared cause. When one model repeatedly fails in a distinctive way, compare its traces with successful attempts.

    Inference Providers serves many open-weight models through the same router, so each fresh model is one more value for -m. Several providers can serve the same model with different quantization and context limits, so it helps to pin one with a suffix such as :deepinfra and record it beside the score.

    Figure 8 shows the raman-lab results for each model.

    Industry observers note that figure 8. raman-lab results per model, with pass@3, pass^3, and the mean pass rate with its clustered standard error. Select a square to inspect that rollout.

    Sources indicate that the comparison makes one pattern in gpt-oss-120b clearer: it often declares completion before seeing command output. In this separate run with DeepInfra pinned as the provider, it called mark_task_complete in its first response in 22 of 24 rollouts, while none of the other five models did so (Figure 9). The Step 6 run used the router's default provider and recorded 19 of 24 such early completions. It passed 11 of 24 rollouts, compared with 13 of 24 in the DeepInfra run. Both counts use the same test: whether the model called mark_task_complete in its first response.

    Figure 9. raman-lab rollout outcomes by when the agent declared completion. Left: the agent observed command output first. Right: it called mark_task_complete in its first response.

    In a recent development, the comparison also shows the limits of the development set. Qwen3.8-27B, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and MiniMax-M3.1-Flash passed all 24 raman-lab rollouts, so these tasks cannot rank them. That will take harder tasks.

    According to recent reports, inference for all six models cost under $5 at the router's list prices. The median raman-lab rollout used about 6,000 tokens for gpt-oss-120b and about 90,000 for MiniMax-M3.1-Flash. The companion repository holds the traces, the per-rollout results, and the scripts to add another model.

    Reusing the runner and task format let us concentrate on the physics, grading, and review. We could reuse them because Harbor and Terminal-Bench publish their code and tasks.

    Task: We reused the Harbor task format and Terminal-Bench's raman-fitting task. The fresh work was a narrower claim, skill coverage, and instructions for raman-lab.

    Task data: The original spectrum served as a starting example. We built a generator for eight spectra with known parameters and reviewed them manually.

    According to recent reports, environment: Harbor's environment support and HF Sandbox ran the tasks. We checked package requirements and diagnosed missing dependencies.

    Agent harness and tools: Terminus-2 with shell access, with Inference Providers for model responses. This part needed no new work.

    Rollout and trace: Harbor's rollout records and ATIF captured each run. We reviewed successes and failures and grouped them by cause.

    Reference solution: We kept the convention of running solution/solve.sh and wrote a reference fit for each newly introduced task.

    Evaluation harness: Harbor ran in an HF Job. We configured the run and grouped results by task.

    Verifier: We reused the tests/test.sh entry point and its way of writing the score to a file. The new work was fit and ratio checks, plus tests for shortcuts and incorrect outputs.

    It has been revealed that agent harness: The software around a model that turns its responses into actions, such as shell commands. Terminus-2 is the agent harness in this post.

    Agentic evaluation: An evaluation that scores what an agent changed in an environment, not only the text it returned.

    ATIF: Agent Trajectory Interchange Format, a shared format for recording an agent's messages, tool calls and observations.

    Canary string: A unique marker in benchmark files that lets model trainers find and exclude them from training data.

    Clustered standard error: A standard error that treats rollouts of the same task as related, which gives a wider and more honest margin than treating each rollout as independent.

    Container image: A fixed package of operating system, files and software, so every rollout starts from the same environment.

    Contamination: Test questions or solutions appearing in training data, so a score may reflect memory rather than skill.

    Context limit: The maximum amount of text, counted in tokens, that a model can read in one request.

    D, G and 2D peaks: Features in graphene's Raman spectrum. G and 2D indicate the number of layers, and D appears when the carbon lattice has defects.

    Sources indicate that defect ratio: The intensity of the D peak divided by that of the G peak, used to indicate defects in graphene. Also called the D-to-G ratio.

    Development set: Tasks used while building and debugging an evaluation, as opposed to a held-back test set used for final scores.

    Environment: The software, files and resources an agent works in during a task.

    Evaluation harness: The software that runs tasks, repeats rollouts, collects traces and aggregates scores. Harbor is the evaluation harness in this post.

    Gated dataset: A Hugging Face dataset that can be downloaded only after the owner approves an access request.

    Harbor: An open-source evaluation harness for agentic tasks.

    In a recent development, HF Job: Compute on Hugging Face that runs a script. Here it runs Harbor.

    HF Sandbox: An isolated Hugging Face environment where a single rollout runs its commands and stores its files.

    Held-out test set: Test items kept private so that models cannot be trained or tuned on them.

    Inference Providers: A Hugging Face service that routes model requests to third-party providers through one API, called the router.

    Lorentzian: A mathematical curve commonly used to model the shape of a spectral peak.

    No-op agent: An agent that does nothing. A sound evaluation gives it a score of zero.

    Open-weight model: A model whose trained parameters are published for anyone to download and run.

    Oracle: An agent that runs the reference solution, used to check that every task can be solved in the supplied environment.

    pass@k: The share of tasks where at least one of k rollouts succeeds.

    pass^k: The share of tasks where all k rollouts succeed.

    Pinning: Fixing the exact versions of software, images or model providers so a run can be repeated.

    Quantization: Storing model weights at lower numerical precision to run faster and cheaper, which can change outputs slightly.

    Raman shift: The difference in frequency between the laser light and the light a sample scatters, measured in cm⁻¹.

    Raman spectroscopy: A technique that shines a laser on a sample and measures shifts in the scattered light to identify properties of the material.

    Reference solution: A known correct way to complete a task, stored with the task.

    In a recent development, rollout: One attempt by an agent at one task. Harbor calls it a trial.

    Run record: A record of what ran behind a score: the exact task, environment, model configuration and code versions.

    Saturation: The point where most models reach top scores on a benchmark, so it no longer separates them.

    Synthetic data: Data generated from known parameters, so the correct answer is known in advance.

    Terminal-Bench: An open benchmark of tasks that an agent completes in a computer terminal.

    Industry observers note that terminus-2: The terminal agent harness used in this post. It connects the model to shell commands.

    Token: The unit of text a model reads and writes, roughly a short word or part of a word.

    Recent findings suggest that trace: The full record of a rollout: the model's messages, its tool calls and what each command returned. Also called a trajectory.

    Verifier: The code that grades a rollout by checking the saved output or the environment's final state.

    #115873. RoboTrack: Point tracking for real-world robotic manipulation

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2340 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    RoboTrack: Point tracking for real-world robotic manipulation

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2340 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 🤖 Models | 📄 Tech Report | 📊 Data | 💻 Code | 🌐 Project Page | 📈 Benchmark.
    • Sources indicate that deploying robots in real-world settings requires reliable perception throughout an interaction.
    • One way to help robots follow these interactions is to track specific locations on the objects they handle.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    🤖 Models | 📄 Tech Report | 📊 Data | 💻 Code | 🌐 Project Page | 📈 Benchmark.

    Sources indicate that deploying robots in real-world settings requires reliable perception throughout an interaction. To pick something up, a robot needs to follow the positions of its gripper and the object as they move. In a laboratory, a robot handling a pipette must keep track of its tip while aligning it with the opening of a tube. These tasks become harder when nearby objects clutter the view, the gripper obscures the object being handled, or the viewing angle changes.

    One way to help robots follow these interactions is to track specific locations on the objects they handle. This is the idea behind point tracking. Given a location in one video frame, a tracker estimates where that same point appears in subsequent frames, when it is occluded, and where it reappears. These trajectories can help robots learn from demonstrations, strategy and guide movements, and model how objects respond to actions.

    Sources indicate that robotics systems often rely on off-the-shelf trackers to automatically annotate motion in videos and provide feedback during execution. And current trackers score well on established robotics benchmarks, suggesting they could be ready for wider use in real-world systems. We wanted to see whether those results hold up across the varied scenes, viewpoints, and object interactions robots encounter in practice.

    Industry observers note that we introduce RoboTrack, a benchmark and training data suite for point tracking in robotic manipulation. RoboTrack-Bench contains 307 human-annotated videos from DROID, Ego-Exo4D, MolmoAct 2, and EgoVerse, covering different robots and human hands, cluttered scenes, and first- and third-person viewpoints. To study how training data affects tracking in these settings, we also extend MolmoSpaces, Ai2’s simulation ecosystem for robot learning, to generate dense point tracks from simulated robot manipulation trajectories. This pipeline produces RoboTrack-15M, a latest synthetic training dataset targeted toward robotic manipulation.

    RoboTrack is a benchmark and training data suite for point tracking in robotic manipulation. Built on MolmoSpaces, RoboTrack-15M (top-left) generates point tracks for training. Training with this simulated data improves tracking on real manipulation footage. RoboTrack-Bench (top-right) provides human-annotated point tracks in real manipulation videos.

    Sources indicate that our evaluations show that leading trackers score much lower on RoboTrack-Bench than on existing robotics benchmarks. Adding RoboTrack-15M to an existing tracker’s training improves performance on real manipulation video, with gains extending to other tracking benchmarks. We bring these pieces together on a real robot, using the resulting tracker to help guide pipette handling in wet-lab tasks.

    According to recent reports, today, we’re releasing both RoboTrack components and two new point tracking models: RoboTracker and RoboTracker-Warp. RoboTracker is a fine-tuned AllTracker model using our techniques and data, while RoboTracker-Warp is trained from CoWTracker. Both models improve average AJ across the three robotics benchmarks compared with their respective released baselines, and RoboTracker-Warp achieves state-of-the-art performance on four out of the five benchmarks we evaluated. We’re also releasing our paper describing the work and evaluation results.

    Recent findings suggest that roboTrack-Bench at a glance. Examples from each source dataset (307 clips and 2,522 human-verified tracks in total). MolmoAct 2 and EgoVerse show one embodiment per panel. DROID and EgoExo4D show synchronized ego (top) and exo (bottom) views.

    According to recent reports, roboTrack-Bench expands evaluation beyond controlled tabletop setups. It contains 307 videos from DROID, Ego-Exo4D, MolmoAct 2, and EgoVerse, annotated with a total of 2,522 point tracks. The videos show robots and human hands manipulating objects across cluttered scenes and first- and third-person viewpoints. Small objects can be difficult to follow against a busy background, and grippers often hide the objects they hold.

    Every track in RoboTrack-Bench is annotated and verified by humans. We ask annotators to prioritize points that move or become occluded rather than the many static background points in robot videos. Following the TAP-Vid annotation approach, annotators use motion estimates to help trace each point through a video. They label each track as belonging to a robot or human body, a manipulated object, or a static object to support future analysis of performance on each group. A second group of annotators checks every track frame by frame before it’s included in our curated data.

    To support research in multi-view pointing, correspondence, and tracking, RoboTrack-Bench contains a subset of 33 video pairs that were recorded simultaneously from two cameras. We annotate the same physical points in both views, synchronized across frames, connecting different views of the same interaction.

    According to recent reports, we evaluated four leading trackers – CoTracker3, BootsTAPNext, AllTracker, and CoWTracker – on RoboTrack-Bench and four other benchmarks: RoboTAP (real-world tabletop manipulation), RGB-Stacking (simulated manipulation), and DAVIS and Kinetics (general video). We report Average Jaccard (AJ), which measures tracking accuracy and visibility prediction; higher scores are better.

    Industry observers note that roboTrack-Bench is harder than existing robot benchmarks. Every final tracker we evaluated scores lower on RoboTrack-Bench than on RoboTAP, the only other real-video robotics benchmark. Their score drops by 3.0 to 6.6 AJ. Even the strongest off-the-shelf tracker, CoWTracker, drops from 70.5 AJ on RoboTAP to 63.9 on RoboTrack-Bench. The drop holds across models despite their different architectures and training data, indicating RoboTrack-Bench identifies weaknesses across multiple trackers.

    RGB-Stacking rewards synthetic training more than real-world ability. BootsTAPNext is TAPNext trained further on 15 million real videos. That extra real-world training raises its RoboTrack-Bench score by 5.1 AJ (55.1 to 60.2), but lowers its RGB-Stacking score by 9.5 AJ (75.0 to 65.5). RGB-Stacking is built from simulated block stacking, and it ranks the Kubric-only model higher, while real manipulation video ranks them the other way around.

    A lead on the older benchmarks does not carry over. CoWTracker leads CoTracker3 by 4.7 AJ on RoboTAP, but by only 2.1 AJ on RoboTrack-Bench. AllTracker’s 2.7-point lead over CoTracker3 on RoboTAP shrinks to 0.8. BootsTAPNext, the strongest model on DAVIS, falls 3.7 AJ behind CoWTracker on RoboTrack-Bench and even trails the Kubric-only AllTracker (60.2 vs 61.4 AJ), despite its training on 15 million real videos.

    These results suggest that existing benchmarks give an incomplete picture of tracking performance in real-world manipulation. Evaluating on more varied scenes reveals difficulties shared by all four trackers and changes how their strengths compare.

    It has been revealed that note: Each tracker runs with its authors’ settings and is all scored in the same way. Our AllTracker scores differ slightly from the published ones because we fixed a scoring bug in its released evaluation code. Additionally, we evaluate RoboTAP and Kinetics on all annotated points rather than following AllTracker’s protocol. See our paper for full evaluation protocols.

    Why do these trackers struggle with real-world manipulation? Many trackers train on synthetic videos generated with Kubric, which shows objects tossed into a scene. These provide examples of motion and occlusion, but don’t focus on robots grasping and moving objects. We wanted to test whether adding trajectories from these interactions could improve tracking on real manipulation videos.

    According to recent reports, this is where MolmoSpaces comes in—our robotic simulation environment at Ai2. We extend its existing manipulation simulations to generate dense point tracks on the robot and the objects it handles. In each episode, a simulated robot arm picks up an everyday object, such as a cup, a plate, or a block. Two cameras record the interaction: one on the wrist and one at the robot’s base, rendered in MuJoCo. Using the simulator’s geometry, object poses, and camera information, we calculate each point’s position and visibility in every frame without human annotation and filter out static points on the background and the robot’s fixed base.

    In a recent development, the pipeline produces RoboTrack-15M for training. RoboTrack-15M has 3,000 videos from 300 simulated homes with 5,000 tracks per video, for 15 million tracks in total.

    Recent findings suggest that data generation pipeline of RoboTrack-15M. Objects, indoor scenes, and robot grasps are obtained from MolmoSpaces. We use the simulator’s geometry and camera information to calculate point positions and visibility.

    Industry observers note that we introduce two models trained on RoboTrack-15M, RoboTracker and RoboTracker-Warp. Each fine-tunes an existing tracker on RoboTrack-15M together with its original training data. RoboTracker builds on AllTracker, a lightweight model with 17 million parameters, and RoboTracker-Warp builds on CoWTracker, a much larger model with about 1 billion parameters.

    According to recent reports, we’re releasing both model checkpoints so other researchers can inspect and build on this work. RoboTracker-Warp’s weights are for noncommercial use.

    Adding RoboTrack-15M improves scores on robotics benchmarks. Compared with the released AllTracker and CoWTracker models, respectively, RoboTracker improves RoboTrack-Bench by 0.8 AJ (62.6 to 63.4) and RoboTracker-Warp by 2.1 AJ (63.9 to 66.0), with gains of up to 1.2 AJ averaged across the three robotics benchmarks. On general video benchmarks, both models perform on par with their base models. Overall, RoboTracker-Warp has the highest AJ of the models we evaluated on four of the five benchmarks. The exception is DAVIS, where BootsTAPNext and CoWTracker score slightly higher.

    Industry observers note that improvements from fine-tuning on RoboTrack-15M, for AllTracker (RoboTracker) and CoWTracker (RoboTracker-Warp). The robotics average is taken over RoboTrack-Bench, RoboTAP, and RGB-Stacking.

    Results on RoboTrack-Bench by video source.

    Breaking the gains down by source highlights where they come from. RoboTracker-Warp improves on every source by roughly 1 to 3 AJ, including the human footage from EgoVerse and Ego-Exo4D, even though RoboTrack-15M contains only robot arms. RoboTracker’s gains are smaller and come mostly from robot footage—clearest on DROID Franka and EgoVerse EVA.

    Recent findings suggest that roboTrack-15M is the result of multiple iterations and experiments with our synthetic data. In fact, our first attempt didn’t bring any gain on RoboTrack-Bench. To find out why, we looked at a simple question: how far do the tracked points move compared with real manipulation videos? We plot this as a histogram for each version of our data and measure its distance from RoboTrack-Bench (figure below).

    In a recent development, how far points move in each version of our training data compared with RoboTrack-Bench, for third-person (top) and first-person (bottom) views. Distance is the Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD) between the two histograms, with 0 indicating identical histograms. Kubric has one camera type, so the same clips appear in both rows. AJ is measured on the full RoboTrack-Bench.

    Industry observers note that the histograms made it clear what was going wrong. Our first version picked points anywhere in the frame, including walls, floors, and furniture, so most points seen from the fixed third-person camera never moved. To address this, we next sampled points only on the robot and the objects it handles, which brought the wrist view close to real video and raised the score. Interestingly, we found that Kubric had the same mismatch in the wrist view, which likely explains why it alone isn’t enough for the varied viewpoints of robotic manipulation. Finally, we moved points from the robot’s fixed base and mounting platform onto the moving arm, which brings our third-person view in line with real video as well and raises the ablation score to 63.0 AJ, 1.5 points above the Kubric-only control.

    Our wet-lab pipeline for guiding the robot with point tracks from a single demonstration.

    What does better point tracking mean for robotics? Many robotic systems have found point tracks useful as a compact representation of how objects move that can guide a policy directly. To see this in practice, we built a similar system for a wet-lab task: pipetting liquid from one vial to another.

    According to recent reports, here, a robot arm picks up an electronic pipette, draws liquid from the first vial, dispenses it into the second, and returns the pipette to its holder. The task is challenging because the pipette tip has to line up with the vial opening within millimeters, and the robot needs to adjust to different layouts of vials in each trial.

    It has been revealed that following RoboTap, the robot learns the task from a single demonstration, which we record by teleoperation and split into steps. At test time, the robot compares what its camera sees with the demonstration and uses RoboTracker to estimate the motion required to align with the vial. Because the following motion runs without further feedback, the task only succeeds if that estimate is accurate.

    We compare three ways of estimating where the vial has moved:.

    We ran each method on 20 layouts with the vials in different positions: 10 with a clear view and 10 with partial occlusion. Point tracking completed the full transfer in 17 of 20 trials, compared with 8 for object masks and 5 for optical flow. It succeeded in all 10 clear-view trials and 7 of 10 with occlusion, where the mask-based method succeeded only once.

    The other methods fail in different ways. Optical flow breaks down when the vials sit far from where they were in the demonstration, and masks can latch onto a similar-looking object or lose the vial when it’s occluded. Point tracking, on the other hand, follows the same vial object from frame to frame, so it handles both large moves and partial occlusion. These results suggest point tracking is a promising tool for precise robotic manipulation tasks.

    It has been revealed that success rate of pipetting trials with each method, with and without occlusion (10 layouts each). A trial counts as a success when the robot completes the full transfer.

    We find the trackers still struggle with long occlusions, finding points when they reappear, and following small objects against busy backgrounds. Training on RoboTrack-15M improves performance, but these failures remain a challenge for real-world use.

    Our simulations also focus on picking up everyday objects. They don't yet capture the precise movements involved in tasks such as pipette handling. A next step is to simulate these tasks more closely and test whether training on their trajectories improves tracking during deployment.

    According to recent reports, roboTrack gives us a way to measure these failures and generate training data to address them. We hope the benchmarks, simulation pipeline, and released model help others build trackers that robots can rely on.

    What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)

    📅 18 Apr 2022 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1066 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Blogspot

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information.
    • It’s like your computer’s hard drive.
    • Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

    It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain.

    Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

    A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

    In a recent development, A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

    Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

    Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

    To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:.

    Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

    According to recent reports, blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

    Sources indicate that and that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more promptly than ever.

    Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

    In a recent development, blockchain already being adopted by some significant-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

    Industry observers note that although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

    Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

    Industry observers note that blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

    Sources indicate that blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

    In a recent development, have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

    Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

    Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

    Recent findings suggest that blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a organization's product inventory.

    Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages.

    I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

    Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

    Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of owners constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

    Sources indicate that coinbase Global is right now the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

    Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

    Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency.

    It has been revealed that generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

    According to recent reports, blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. Hope you like this article if you have any question let me know in the comments section.

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1413 w)

    Microduck Obstacle Avoidance: A Sim2Real Workflow with Isaac Lab and Newton

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1413 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Add local obstacle avoidance to Microduck while keeping its walking policy fixed.
    • Recent findings suggest that A walking policy can keep Microduck balanced, but it does not tell the robot how to steer around an obstacle in its path.
    • According to recent reports, NVIDIA Isaac Lab is an open-source framework for training policies across thousands of GPU-parallel simulations and it provides the robot-learning environment.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Add local obstacle avoidance to Microduck while keeping its walking policy fixed. Build varied courses with reusable SimReady assets, model ToF sensing with Newton’s raycaster, and train a controller in Isaac Lab to adjust gamepad velocity commands around obstacles. This tutorial covers simulation training, evaluation, export, and real-robot deployment.

    Recent findings suggest that A walking policy can keep Microduck balanced, but it does not tell the robot how to steer around an obstacle in its path. In this workflow, we reuse the walking policy from our first Microduck tutorial and keep its weights fixed. This follow-up trains a separate avoidance controller using time-of-flight (ToF) sensing. You choose a direction with a gamepad; the controller adjusts the velocity command before passing it to the walking policy.

    According to recent reports, NVIDIA Isaac Lab is an open-source framework for training policies across thousands of GPU-parallel simulations and it provides the robot-learning environment. Newton simulates physics and the sensor’s depth measurements. We will cover the control architecture, train on varied obstacle layouts, evaluate the resulting policies, and prepare the interface for hardware testing.

    For simulation and training, prepare:.

    According to recent reports, A Linux system with a compatible NVIDIA GPU and driver. See the Isaac Lab installation guide for platform requirements.

    Git with Git LFS, and the uv package manager.

    For physical-robot testing, prepare:.

    A configured Microduck. Load the same backlash walking-policy export used by the navigation task.

    A supported ToF sensor with its configuration recorded.

    A paired gamepad and a level test area with obstacles.

    Install uv if it is not already installed. Then clone the exp/microduck branch of the Isaac Lab repository and install its dependencies:.

    Once setup is complete, list the available Microduck environments and presets:.

    Download and export the upstream backlash walking checkpoint once before training. The obstacle avoidance task loads the exported walking policy automatically.

    It has been revealed that the environment combines simple primitives with OpenUSD assets available through SimReady Central on Hugging Face. We use a cardboard box, office bin, bedside cabinet alongside cones. From the IsaacLab repository root, download the pinned box, bin and cabinet packages into assets/simready.

    At each episode reset, the environment code automatically samples a layout, shuffles the props, and varies their placement and rotation. Most courses scatter obstacles ahead of the duck, with a smaller mix of clear paths, barriers and passages. The code also mirrors layouts and mixes aligned and staggered rows.

    Goals start ahead of the duck. Movement commands guide it toward the goal while the policy adjusts them around obstacles.

    Figure 1. Varied obstacle-course layouts with SimReady assets and primitive geometry.

    According to recent reports, the IsaacContrib-ObstacleAvoidance-Flat-MicroDuck task separates obstacle avoidance from balance. A navigation policy uses ToF sensing to adjust forward, lateral, and yaw commands at 50 Hz. The frozen walking policy then converts those commands into joint actions, allowing the robot to learn obstacle avoidance without retraining its walking behavior.

    During training, the navigation policy’s actor receives ToF history and body and controller state available on the real robot. Its critic has access to additional simulation state to guide learning, but is not needed for deployment.

    Sources indicate that rewards encourage progress toward the goal, safe arrivals, and movement around obstacles. Following a movement command earns credit only when the robot makes progress with sufficient clearance; risky approaches reduce that credit. Penalties discourage fast approaches, abrupt command changes, collisions, and falls.

    Sources indicate that the obstacle-avoidance task lives in isaaclab_tasks.contrib.microduck_obstacle. Its configuration is in obstacle_avoidance_env_cfg.py, ToF sensing is in sensors.py, and actions, commands, observations and rewards are organized under mdp/.

    Recent findings suggest that microDuckToFCamera extends Newton’s LegacyMultiMeshRayCasterCamera to model the VL53L5CX—a compact time-of-flight (ToF) sensor on the microduck that measures distance across an 8×8 grid at 15Hz. The simulated sensor has a 45° field of view and a 0.12–4 m range. It follows the duck’s head, with placement similar to the sensor on the real duck.

    Real recordings informed the sensor placement and floor readings in simulation. Training adds noise, delays and missing measurements—including near the grid’s edges—to expose the policy to imperfect data. The excerpt below highlights selected sensor settings already included in the task configuration. You do not need to edit or run this code separately.

    Train the navigation policy with PPO across 16,384 parallel environments for 1,500 training iterations. Its actor, critic, normalizers, and optimizer start fresh. The task configuration loads the fixed walking checkpoint, robot model, and obstacle assets.

    The 16,384 environments shown here are configurable, not a minimum requirement. Lower --num_envs to fit your GPU’s available memory. With fewer environments collecting experience in parallel, reaching comparable policy performance may require more training iterations and longer training time. We also trained this policy on NVIDIA DGX Spark in approximately 6 hours using 4,096 parallel environments for 3,000 PPO updates, demonstrating a smaller-scale configuration for the same workflow.

    Run this command to train the policy:.

    According to recent reports, figure 2. Parallel MicroDuck obstacle-avoidance simulation.

    Playback uses the same props, primitives, frozen walker and sensor randomization as training, with a different seed for fresh obstacle arrangements.

    Recent findings suggest that navigation checkpoints are saved under logs/rsl_rl/microduck_obstacle_avoidance_tof_flat_backlash// relative to the repository root. Choose a model_.pt file from your run and replace /absolute/path/to/model.pt below with its path. This plays the policy, opens the Newton viewer and records 20 seconds of simulation. Set --viz to none for headless recording.

    Playback saves TorchScript and ONNX models in the checkpoint’s exported folder. Keep the ONNX data file alongside the model.

    According to recent reports, figure 3. Cone-course evaluation with requested motion, policy steering, and ToF input overlays.

    These deployment tools run the navigation model on a laptop and send adjusted gamepad commands to the walking policy on the robot. Use the same walking policy that was used during navigation training.

    Section 1 saves the walker’s ONNX export to .pretrained_checkpoints/rsl_rl/https/omniverse-content-production.s3-us-west-2.amazonaws.com/Assets/Isaac/6.2/Isaac/IsaacLab/PretrainedCheckpoints/rsl_rl/exported/policy.onnx, relative to the Isaac Lab repository root.

    Load that walking policy using Pollen’s policy-loading guide. The deployment README includes the transfer steps, including how to package an ONNX export that uses an external data file.

    From your Isaac Lab checkout, set up SSH access and check inference with the robot standing upright and still:.

    Sources indicate that dry-run copies the helpers and streams sensor data, but sends no movement commands. Watch the proposed commands as obstacles enter the sensor’s view. Keep the navigation ONNX and any companion .data file together.

    Once those checks pass, start supervised gamepad navigation:.

    Recent findings suggest that hold the stick forward to request movement; the policy adjusts the command to avoid obstacles. Release the stick to stop, press X to toggle navigation, and use Ctrl-C to end the session. Forward speed is capped at 0.15 m/s by default, with an additional close-obstacle brake and stale-input stopping. Start in a clear area and verify stopping before testing a course.

    See the deployment README for controls, logs and troubleshooting.

    Figure 4. Microduck steers around cones using its 8×8 ToF sensor, with real footage on the left and a 3D rebuild from its logs on the right. Blue shows the policy steering, purple shows the operator intervention.

    Sources indicate that the Microduck task collection includes velocity tracking on flat and rough terrain; stand-up recovery, sit–stand transitions, and walking with fall recovery (VelStand); ball kicking, ground picking, and forward rolls (Roulade). Roller-skating tasks add velocity tracking and swizzle motion, crouch-gliding, slope descent, standing up on skates, and spins.

Explore new behaviors by changing commands, rewards, or environments—from rough-terrain walking to perception-driven obstacle avoidance. Evaluate your policy on scenes outside the training set before testing on the robot.

    O preço mínimo mente: como citar preços de um mercado cheio de outliers

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that eu mantenho um índice de preços diário de painéis SMM, as lojas atacadistas que vendem seguidores, curtidas e visualizações por milhar.
    • A primeira versão publicava exatamente isso.
    • Curtidas de Instagram, também 87 painéis: mediana de 0,56, máximo bruto de 384.000.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that eu mantenho um índice de preços diário de painéis SMM, as lojas atacadistas que vendem seguidores, curtidas e visualizações por milhar. Todo dia o sistema lê os catálogos de cerca de 90 painéis, converte cada oferta para dólares por 1.000 unidades e calcula, para cada serviço, o mínimo, os quartis, a mediana e o máximo.

    A primeira versão publicava exatamente isso. E o primeiro problema apareceu no primeiro dia: o mínimo e o máximo eram inúteis. Este post é sobre por quê, e sobre a regra que usamos no lugar deles.

    Seguidores de Instagram, 87 painéis na amostra:.

    Curtidas de Instagram, também 87 painéis: mediana de 0,56, máximo bruto de 384.000.

    According to recent reports, ninguém vende 1.000 seguidores por um centésimo de centavo, e ninguém cobra cem mil dólares por eles. Essas linhas existem nos catálogos, mas não são preços:.

    Se um jornalista escreve "seguidores custam de US$ 0,0001 a US$ 100.000", a frase é tecnicamente verdadeira e completamente errada.

    Sources indicate that com um máximo de 100.000 numa amostra de 87, a média de seguidores de Instagram passaria de mil dólares. A mediana não se mexe: uma linha absurda a mais ou a menos desloca a posição do meio em no máximo uma oferta.

    O mercado também é bimodal em vários serviços. Inscritos de YouTube têm uma camada de bots, barata e sem reposição, e uma camada com garantia de reposição que custa dezenas de vezes mais. Uma média entre as duas descreve um produto que ninguém vende. Por isso o índice publica a mediana e o intervalo P25–P75, que é onde estão as opções de um comprador normal.

    Para o "mais barato" e o "mais caro" usamos uma regra simples:.

    A faixa citável é a oferta mais barata e a mais cara dentro de dez vezes a mediana do serviço, deixando de fora os pacotes de pedido único.

    Para seguidores de Instagram hoje: US$ 0,38 a US$ 38,00, contra o bruto de 0,0001 a 100.000. Para curtidas: 0,057 a 5,60.

    O CSV mantém as duas colunas de propósito. Os extremos brutos ficam para quem quer auditar; a página e a API orientam a citar a mediana, os quartis e a faixa citável.

    In a recent development, dez vezes é uma ordem de grandeza. É largo o bastante para manter as ofertas premium que são produtos reais, como seguidores com geolocalização ou com garantia de reposição, e estreito o bastante para deixar de fora os extremos brutos, que erram por fatores muito maiores: numa medição de 7 de novembro, em 89 de 149 serviços o extremo bruto passava de 100 vezes a mediana.

    Recent findings suggest that A mesma ideia aparece no ranking de preço dos painéis: cada serviço é comparado com a mediana do seu próprio mercado, e razões fora de 0,02× a 20× são descartadas como erro de dado ou produto diferente com o mesmo nome. A regra completa está na metodologia.

    Tudo sob CC BY 4.0. Se você citar um número, cite a mediana e a data.

    Transparência: eu mantenho o PanelCompare. O site tem um espaço patrocinado identificado e links de afiliado; nenhum dos dois entra no cálculo dos preços.
